desc:
A postfix (reverse Polish) expression is stored as an integer array tokens. The values 100001, 100002, 100003 and 100004 stand for the binary operators +, -, * and /; every other token is an operand with absolute value at most 100,000. An operator is written after its two operands: [7, 2, 100002] is 7 - 2.

Evaluate the expression and return its value. Division discards the fractional part, i.e. it rounds toward zero (7 / 2 = 3, -7 / 2 = -3).

The expression is always valid, no division by zero happens, and every intermediate result fits in a signed 32-bit integer.

Examples: [2, 1, 100001, 3, 100003] is (2 + 1) * 3 = 9. [4, 13, 5, 100004, 100001] is 4 + (13 / 5) = 6. [-7, 2, 100004] is -3.
constraints: tokens is a valid postfix expression; operators are 100001 (+), 100002 (-), 100003 (*), 100004 (/)
No division by zero; every intermediate value is within [-(2<sup>31</sup> - 1), 2<sup>31</sup> - 1]
hints: In postfix notation the two operands of an operator are the two values computed just before it.
Use a stack: push every operand. When you meet an operator, pop two values, combine them and push the result.

Mind the order: the value popped first is the right operand. Subtraction and division need second_popped op first_popped. For division, compute with absolute values and fix the sign, because floor division rounds negative results the wrong way.
editorial: Postfix notation was designed for stacks. Walk through the tokens from left to right. An operand is pushed. An operator takes the two most recent finished values: pop b (the right operand), then pop a (the left operand), compute a op b and push it back. When all tokens are consumed the stack holds one value, the answer.

The only subtle part is division. Python's // rounds toward negative infinity, but the problem asks to round toward zero. Compute q = abs(a) // abs(b) and give it a minus sign when exactly one of a, b is negative.
Every token is processed once with O(1) work, so the time is O(n); the stack can hold up to O(n) values.
